n: Azariah (Uzziah) becomes king of Judah. The synchronism with Jeroboam II’s 27th year likely reflects overlapping co-regencies, which make biblical dates complex.
He took the throne at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years (about 792–740 BC, including co-regencies)—one of Judah’s longest reigns. Isaiah’s call came in the year he died.
He did right, following his father’s good example.
Yet the hilltop shrines remained.

The Lord struck him with a skin disease, and he lived isolated in a separate house while his son Jotham governed. Chronicles explains why: in pride he tried to burn incense in the temple, a duty reserved for priests.

f.g: a separate house, an isolation dwelling.
in charge of the palace; acting ruler.

n: His deeds—military, agricultural, and building successes—are recorded in Judah’s chronicles and summarized in 2 Chronicles 26.

f.w: the rest of the acts of Azariah

n: Azariah dies and his son Jotham succeeds him.
Now the account turns to Israel’s collapse. Zachariah, Jeroboam II’s son, reigns just six months (about 753 BC).
He continued Jeroboam I’s sins.
Shallum assassinates him publicly and takes the throne.
Zachariah’s deeds are in Israel’s annals.
The narrator notes that the Lord’s promise to Jehu—four generations on the throne—was exactly fulfilled: Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II, and Zachariah.
Shallum reigns only one month.
Menahem marches from Tirzah, the old capital, kills Shallum, and seizes the throne. Israel has entered a spiral of assassinations—four of its last six kings were murdered.
Shallum’s brief reign and plot are recorded in the annals.
Menahem savagely attacks the town of Tiphsah because it refused to open its gates to him, even killing pregnant women. Israel’s kings now act like the cruelest foreign invaders.

f.g: possibly a town near Tirzah; some versions read Tappuah.

n: Menahem rules ten years (about 752–742 BC).
He too clings to Jeroboam’s sins.
Pul—another name for the great Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III—invades. Menahem pays a huge tribute to secure Assyrian backing for his rule. Assyrian records list Menahem among the tributaries.

f.g: the Babylonian throne name of Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745–727 BC).

n: Menahem raises the money by taxing about 60,000 wealthy landowners fifty shekels each. Assyria withdraws—for now.
His deeds are recorded in Israel’s annals.
Menahem dies; his son Pekahiah succeeds him.
Pekahiah reigns two years (about 742–740 BC).
He continues in Jeroboam’s sins.
Pekah, his officer, leads fifty men from Gilead in a palace coup and kills him. Pekah likely represented an anti-Assyrian faction.
Pekahiah’s deeds are in the annals.
Pekah reigns twenty years—a figure many scholars think counts years when he ruled a rival territory in Gilead before taking Samaria.
He, too, follows Jeroboam’s sins.
Tiglath-pileser III invades about 733 BC, conquers Galilee and Gilead, and deports their people to Assyria—the first stage of the northern kingdom’s exile.

f.g: the tribal area west of the Sea of Galilee.

n: Hoshea assassinates Pekah and becomes Israel’s last king. Assyrian records claim Tiglath-pileser placed Hoshea on the throne.

f.g: counting from Jotham’s co-regency; the synchronism is complex.

n: Pekah’s deeds are recorded in the annals.
Back in Judah, Jotham becomes king in Pekah’s second year.
He was twenty-five and reigned sixteen years (counting his co-regency with Uzziah). His mother was likely from a priestly family.

f.g: possibly from the priestly family of Zadok.

n: Jotham did right, like his father.
The high places remained, but he built the Upper Gate of the temple.

f.g: the upper gate, probably on the north side of the temple courts.

n: His deeds are recorded in Judah’s chronicles.
The Lord begins to send Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel against Judah—the Syro-Ephraimite crisis that Isaiah addresses in Isaiah 7.
Jotham dies and his son Ahaz becomes king.
